extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers, university professors, curriculum designers, and math educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for how mathematics should be taught at school and university levels, emphasizing connections with physics, concrete examples, modelling, and historical/motivated introductions rather than pure axiomatic formalisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as part of physics / experimental science
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is a part of physics and a part of natural science; 'Mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach mathematics through experiments, examples and observations; present mathematical facts as discoverable phenomena (like the Jacobi identity) comparable to empirical findings. Avoid treating mathematics as wholly divorced from experimental reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach modelling and its limits (idealisation and validation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model construction involves idealisation (treating probabilistic/approximate facts as 'axioms') and thus models must be treated with caution because small parameter changes can drastically change conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly teach the relative character of axioms, the sensitivity of models to initial conditions (example: limits on long-term weather forecasts; uniqueness theorem in Malthus equation), and insist on validating models by experiments or counterexamples. Warn students that long chains of deduction decrease reliability and that modelling assumptions must be checked in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer observation–model–test scientific scheme over definition–theorem–proof alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The physics/scientific scheme (observation → model → investigation of model → conclusions → testing by observations) is more appropriate for mathematical education than merely definition–theorem–proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching, start from observations and motivating examples, then build models and test them; avoid replacing the scientific approach by unmotivated axiomatic presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic/abstract‑only teaching (anti‑axiomatisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutting mathematics off from physics (scholastic, super‑abstract mathematics) makes it unfit for teaching and application and breeds dislike and misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not teach abstract axioms as ends in themselves. Avoid presenting artificial or obscure axiomatic constructions to beginners; instead ground concepts in concrete reality and applications. Anti‑pattern: asking a child 'what is 2+3?' and receiving '3+2, since addition is commutative'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with concrete, geometric and visual intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry, pictures and physical interpretations (e.g., determinant as oriented volume, graphs of parametric curves, paraboloids) should play a central role in teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce objects visually and by interpretation: show determinants as volumes, draw curves given parametrically, present Riemann surfaces concretely. Use drawings, physical analogies and geometric examples before formal abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce concepts historically and motivatively (definitions from use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer historically motivated or operational definitions (e.g., transformation view of groups; manifold as embedded submanifold) to dry axiom‑first definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why a concept was invented and how it arose from problems; for groups, start with transformations and their composition/inverses; for manifolds, present as subsets of Euclidean space locally given as graphs. Avoid imposing long lists of abstract axioms before motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach key theorems that reveal deep connections and wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Include theorems that expose unity across mathematics and give emotional/significant insight (examples: classification of surfaces; Jacobi connections; Abel addition theorem; Riemann surfaces and integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such theorems (even without full proofs) to inspire students and show the richness of mathematics. Prefer theorems that build correct Weltanschauung and connect to applications over 'sporting' or exotic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train concrete mathematical craft and problem‑solving skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must be able to perform basic craft tasks (e.g., drawing curves, solving parametric problems, counting arguments that motivate algebraic facts) as part of the mathematician's skill set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include practice with hands‑on problems (drawing xy = z^2 surfaces, parametric curve plotting, counting arguments to see commutativity) to develop intuition and competence; these are as essential as knowing times tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize cross‑connections between heterogeneous objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight surprising links (e.g., same function relating sums of squares and pendulum motion; elliptic integrals appearing in dynamics) to show mathematics' unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach instances where apparently different domains are related and use these to motivate study and research; exploit analogies to kindle curiosity and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and experiments to detect and combat errors in long arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Long deductive chains are error‑prone (sign mistakes, symbol misplacement): external control by examples/experiments is the technology to combat such errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students habitually to check proofs and computations with concrete examples and numerical tests; encourage computational experiments and sanity checks as routine practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple models; avoid unnecessary complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex models are rarely useful (unless for those writing dissertations); overcomplexity often leads to self‑deception and reduced applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simpler models that capture essential behavior; avoid building overly elaborate formal structures without demonstrable practical or explanatory gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide physical interpretations of abstract constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract algebraic or analytic notions should be tied to physical/geometric meaning (e.g., determinant = oriented volume; commutativity via rectangle area computations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing abstract concepts, first give concrete physical or geometric interpretations so students see why these notions matter and how they arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select classical, methodical texts and historically strong expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many older, well‑written books (Rademacher & Toeplitz; Hilbert & Cohn‑Vossen; Courant & Robbins; Polya; Klein; Hermite; Landau & Lifshitz) present mathematics in a methodical, motivating way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use and recommend such books in courses and curricula rather than discarding them for modern sterile textbooks; these texts help maintain connection to applications and intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promoting 'sporting achievements' as the core of mathematics education
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting exotic, narrowly technical results as the pinnacle of mathematics misleads students and the public and does not foster appreciation or usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus curriculum on results that have explanatory power, broad connections, or real‑world relevance, rather than on isolated hard results that function as intellectual sport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach topology/geometry and classification results early where they inform intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Important classification results (e.g., classification of closed two‑dimensional manifolds) give correct impressions of modern mathematics and should be included even at high‑school/university levels (possibly without full proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate such material to build intuition about the shape and structure of mathematical objects; do not banish geometry from curricula.
